record.paper_title: Finite translation generalized quadrangles: old results, new results, open problems
record.original_question: For pseudo-ovals O(n, n, q) with q even, Theorem 5.7 assumes 2-transitivity in order to characterize classicality. How far can that hypothesis be weakened—for example, would transitivity alone already force the pseudo-oval to be classical?

evidence.quote: 7. Weaken the hypothesis of Theorem 5.7 for q even (e.g., “what about transitive pseudo-ovals?”).
Theorem 5.7. The pseudo-oval O(n, n, q), q even, is classical if and only if O(n, n, q) is 2-transitive.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be an even prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. A pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ is a set of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ such that any three of them span the whole space. The pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}$ is called classical (or elementary, arising from a conic) if there exists a conic $C$ in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ such that, after applying field reduction from $\mathrm{GF}(q^n)$ to $\mathrm{GF}(q)$, the points of $C$ become precisely the elements of $\mathcal{O}$.

The collineation stabiliser $G\le \mathrm{P}\Gamma\mathrm{L}(3n,q)$ of $\mathcal{O}$ is said to act $2$-transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if for any two ordered pairs of distinct elements of $\mathcal{O}$ there is an element of $G$ sending the first pair to the second; it acts transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if any single element of $\mathcal{O}$ can be mapped to any other.

It is known that, for $q$ even, $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ is classical if and only if it admits a $2$-transitive collineation group.

Question: Can the hypothesis of $2$-transitivity be weakened to mere transitivity? That is, is every pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ with $q$ even that admits a transitive collineation group necessarily classical?
artifact.status_search_result: Significant partial progress has been made. Bamberg–Penttila ("Transitive eggs", 2006) and subsequent work by Bamberg, Glasby, Popiel and Praeger (2016) showed that a pseudo-oval (not an oval) admitting an insoluble transitive collineation group is elementary, arising via field reduction from a conic, an elliptic quadric, or a Suzuki–Tits ovoid. Rottey and Van de Voorde (arXiv:1701.09126) classified regular pseudo-ovals in even characteristic for prime $n$. However, the full question—whether transitivity alone (without insolubility or regularity hypotheses) forces classicality of $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in even characteristic—does not appear to have been settled in full generality.

status_evidence.title: Transitive eggs
status_evidence.snippet: A pseudo-oval or pseudo-ovoid admitting an insoluble transitive group of collineations is elementary and arises from a conic, an elliptic quadric, or a Suzuki-Tits ovoid.
status_evidence.claim: Under the extra assumption of insolubility, transitivity implies elementary (and hence classical when arising from a conic).

status_evidence.title: Generalized Quadrangles and Transitive Pseudo-Hyperovals
status_evidence.snippet: A pseudo-hyperoval with an irreducible transitive stabilizer is elementary.
status_evidence.claim: Partial classification of transitive pseudo-(hyper)ovals under irreducibility hypothesis.

status_evidence.title: Regular pseudo-hyperovals and regular pseudo-ovals in even characteristic
status_evidence.snippet: Rottey and Van de Voorde characterized regular pseudo-ovals of PG(3n-1, q), q=2^h, h>1, n prime.
status_evidence.claim: Further partial progress in even characteristic under regularity assumption.
